va_high_knob_landform.blurb: High Knob Landform is a broad massif in the far southwest corner of Virginia, within the Cumberland Mountains, rising to roughly 4,200 feet across parts of Wise, Scott and Lee counties. The rock is hard, fine sandstone, and the area is overwhelmingly a bouldering destination, with a small number of bolted routes on the side. Problems run from V0 up to the V10 range, with a deep supply of V2 to V5 lines and a thinner tail of harder ones. It splits into an East side, home to a large boulderfield with the Labyrinth and Flag Rock, and a West side. The summit is among the wettest and snowiest spots in the state, so expect damp weather.

wa_san_juan_fidalgo_whidbey_islands.blurb: This grouping covers the climbing around the islands of northwest Washington, and nearly all of it is on Mount Erie, the highest point of Fidalgo Island, a few minutes from Anacortes. Erie is built from diorite and offers top-rope, sport, trad and some multipitch on a fairly compact set of crags with short approaches. Most routes fall between 5.7 and 5.11, with plenty of moderates for newer leaders and a handful of 5.12 and 5.13 lines. There is also some bouldering around Fidalgo, much of it undeveloped and needing cleanup. Sitting in the Olympic rain shadow, the area often stays drier than its surroundings, and April to October is the usual window. Deception Pass and the smaller islands add only a little climbing.

mn_duluth_rock_climbs.blurb: Rock outcrops run right through the city of Duluth, which gives its climbing an unusually urban feel. Bouldering makes up the bulk of it, much of it on blocks close to city roads, with problems from V0 to about V6 in good numbers and a few harder ones. Roped climbing is a smaller part of the picture: top-rope walls such as Whopee Wall and Point O' Rocks, a few sport lines and some trad, mostly in the 5.6 to 5.12 range. Other spots need longer walks through woods or along streams. Tettegouche's Palisade Head and Shovel Point lie farther up the North Shore for those wanting bigger roped cliffs.

vt_2_central_vermont.blurb: Central Vermont gathers lightly visited cragging and a lot of bouldering around Killington and Lake Dunmore. Bouldering is the main event, with moderates plentiful from V0 to V5 and a steady tail up to V10 or so; the Killington boulders include many glacial erratics. Roped routes are split between trad and sport, from about 5.3 to 5.12. At Lake Dunmore the crags sit beside the water on hard, fine-grained quartzite, mostly slabby, with lines in the 5.5 to 5.9 range plus a steeper wall and a small boulder area. Eagle Hollow leans toward sport. A handful of ice lines complete the picture. Crowds are light and most areas are spread out.

wa_echo_basin.blurb: Echo Basin is a canyon of basalt columns and pillars next to Frenchman Coulee, near Vantage in central Washington. The Sunshine Wall holds the tallest pillars in the Vantage area and most of the trad, while the lower cliffs, Riverview Area and Powerhouse Area lean toward bolts. Sport and trad are close to evenly split, with routes from about 5.4 to 5.12 and a good run of moderates and 5.10s. The basalt can be loose, so a helmet is wise. The Vantage area is dry and sunny, which makes it a favorite for very early and very late in the season, though deep winter can still turn bitterly cold.

ca_bowman_emeralds.blurb: Bowman/Emeralds is a scatter of crags along the I-80 corridor of the Tahoe region, at around 4,500 to 4,700 feet. The Emeralds and Bowman Valley hold most of the climbing, and bolted sport routes dominate, mostly from 5.8 through 5.12 with a cluster of 5.10 to 5.12. Cracks are scarce, and trad, top-rope and drytooling climbing make up a small share. Island Lake Boulders and the Emeralds add a fair amount of bouldering from V0 to V9. Because of the modest elevation, spring and fall are the best seasons at the Emeralds, where most walls face northwest and give morning shade in summer. Winter typically buries the area in snow.
